source: Cambodia National IPM Program (MAFF Department of Agricultural Extension), in cooperation with FAO — "Cabbage Integrated Pest Management: An Ecological Guide" (adapted from J.W. Ketelaar & A.L.M. Abubakar), August 2008, 266 pages, Chapter 1 section 1.3
text:
The FAO-IPM Inter-Country Programme originally began in rice fields before being extended to vegetable crops, and the vegetable IPM approach shares much of its underlying framework with rice IPM, adapted for vegetables' different growing conditions. Vegetable and rice cropping differ in ways that shaped how the approach had to change: rice varieties and practices are generally well established and locally adapted, with a comparatively more stable field ecosystem, whereas vegetable varieties (including cabbage) are often introduced from outside the country and are less locally adapted, with a less-established field ecosystem that makes the natural pest/predator balance less reliable.

A comparison table in the source contrasts rice and vegetable production across four lines: (1) origin of varieties -- rice varieties are generally domestic/local in origin, while vegetable varieties often come from external/foreign sources; (2) local adaptation -- rice is described as genuinely well-adapted to local soil and conditions, while vegetables are described as not showing the same degree of adaptation; (3) ecosystem stability -- rice fields are described as having a comparatively more stable ecosystem, while vegetable fields are described as less stable; (4) management approach -- rice management is described as not requiring heavy ongoing intervention, while vegetable management is described as needing more active, ongoing management as pest pressure builds.

Because vegetable pests can build up and spread crop damage faster than in rice, and because the vegetable field ecosystem is less self-regulating, the source describes vegetable IPM as shifting away from rice IPM's more 'informed non-intervention' stance (observe first, and only step in once monitoring confirms a real threshold has been crossed) toward an 'informed intervention' approach for vegetables -- acting on field observations before pest pressure has a chance to build into serious crop loss, rather than waiting passively.
caveat: This source is a 266-page FAO/MAFF IPM manual for cabbage (cabbage Source D); this file covers only section 1.3 (page 3 of the source's own pagination). The exact wording of the ecosystem-stability and management-strategy rows of the rice-vs-vegetable comparison table was difficult to read with full confidence from the scan; the qualitative direction of the comparison (rice more stable/less intervention, vegetables less stable/more active management) is clear, but the precise phrasing has been paraphrased rather than quoted.
